title: CLO Master Express Lesson 25 Sweater Teaching Live Replay
description: The long-awaited sweater tutorial is here～ Let’s start learning!!
transcript:
Hello everyone, welcome to today's live broadcast. I am today’s anchor, Lidia. Let's test the sound first—can you hear me?  
If you can hear me, please call out. I see someone calling; that should be no problem. OK, now let's get into the explanation of this live broadcast. Today, I want to take you through how to make a sweater in CLO.  

First, let's look at the production process of our sweater.  
I will make a complete sweater and then introduce the workflow. After that, I'll show you the effect of our sweater.  

First of all, here is our whole sweater. As you can see in the picture, our sweater is divided into four types.  
The first type is cut and sew, which means cutting and sewing the fabric pieces together. This is one way of making a sweater and one of the three main garment construction methods.  

The second method is to sew each fabric piece separately without cutting but sewing them together afterward; this includes the pattern as part of the side material.  

The third method is very similar to the second, but the difference is that the pattern on the bottom and the fabric piece are sewn together. This is the third method.  

The fourth method is a one-piece shape; it does not require matching processes and is sewn together as a whole.  

All four methods are made in 3D in the first method. We can use this 3D model to show details of our sweater, such as the flower collections, 3D organization, and characteristics of our gauze line. We use these to express the design of our sweater.  

Now, let's look at the workflow of our sweater. There are three parts here:  
The first part is digitalization. Digitalization means using other design software to create our DXF paper pattern or making a pattern board. Because in CLO, you need a board to create 3D clothing.  

The next part is physicalization. This means scanning our image. If you don’t have a paper pattern, you can scan a real paper pattern. Then, in CLO, we can use the obtained paper pattern to create some details in CLO.  

It’s also acceptable to draw the pattern board manually.  

The second step is to simulate the physical properties of the fabric of our sweater.  

The third step is our physical processing.  

We will discuss these three parts one by one.  

First, the paper sample: there are four ways to prepare our paper sample.  
The first way, as mentioned earlier, is to use 2D CAD software or other 3D software to generate our paper sample.  

The second way is to adjust a DXF paper sample created by other software. In fact, you can also take some of your existing basic paper samples and then do some design modifications. I will also use this second method to create our first basic sweater today.  

The third way is to draw the paper sample directly in CLO according to the size of the supply unit.  

The fourth way is to collate paper samples; that is, you can have a paper sample and import it into CLO, then use one of our samples to collate our paper sample.  

Next, let's open one of our basic 3D clothing models in the software. Today, I will use this basic model as the starting point to design my sweater.  

First, I found this basic model a little small in size, so my first step is to increase the chest volume. I collapse the basic chest line into our inner line and then align it to the outer line of the board. This step prepares for later operations.  

After aligning, we cut the inner line, perform cut and sew, and then simulate.  

In the 3D window, find the shrink line tool. This tool allows direct clothing design manipulation in the 3D window. I have a division line here that I can adjust by pulling to change the board’s dimension.  

To see the specific adjustment value, I press Shift + Z to display the line length of the board.  

In the 2D window, you can see a specific shrink value. Suppose I want to shrink it by 25, which is 2.5 centimeters (one circle is 10 centimeters). The whole board will have joint modification.  

After shrinking, I want to adjust the length of this board using the moving shape line tool and select the bottom part in the 2D window, moving it about two centimeters shorter. You can see the joint effect of the whole circle.  

Now, I’m going to change the shape of the neck. First, I delete the small collar board on top, then use the edge shape line tool to select the neck points and drag them, referring to the 2D value. The 3D view also provides an intuitive display. I adjust it to a satisfactory size.  

My sleeve is a little thinner than desired, so I want to make it thicker. I cut the sleeve line into a loop, similar to the chest circumference treatment. If you haven’t used our shape line tool before, it’s one of our newer, very convenient functions that allow direct 3D adjustments. I added this feature during preparation.  

Using the shrinked shape line, I enlarge the sleeve for a thicker effect.  

Next, let’s adjust the collar shape. The collar is currently not very round, so I’ll teach you a new tool for length comparison between plates. We select two points, right-click, move plates, and then use the adjustment circle tool to make the arc more rounded. This can be done in 3D but is easier to teach using this method.  

After rotating the plate, we can also rotate it in the direction of the gusset, another new function.  

After changes, we merge the breast line in the middle and simulate.  

At the bottom, we add a gusset structure: using the built-in line tool, we create a 60mm (6cm) wide gusset, delete extra points, then select, cut and sew, and adjust the gusset to vertical because our gusset is straight. All plates are adjusted to vertical to maintain a straight shape for this sweater.  

Now, for the collar gusset, we use the lift tool (shortcut key S). First, I measure the collar length, then input a slightly smaller length because the gusset tightens, and set the width to 60 (half size). I align and edit the other half, then sew.  

After sewing, the gusset collar is loose, so I shorten it to 80% of the original length. Because the collar is a straight plate, it opens at the bottom, so I perform an end-to-end shrinkage to 80% and simulate. This produces a more appropriate gusset collar effect.  

For other design changes, I open my final model and make adjustments using 3D and 2D tools. I apply end-to-end shrinkage of 90% to the gusset collar and simulate. This completes the basic production.  

Next, we assign physical attributes suitable for the sweater fabric. In the CLO fabric library, various knit fabrics are available. We select a fabric type close to the actual sample for simulation. I list four types:  

1. Super fine knit effect - soft, called needle silk knit fabric.  
2. Fine knit effect - needle cotton knit fabric.  
3. Medium-thick knit - Roman knit.  
4. Thickest knit - needle hair circle cloth.  

I choose the thick needle fabric for my sweater. I drag the needle hair circle cloth fabric onto the wooden fabric. I delete the texture and hairline pictures since I only want the physical properties. Holding the Ctrl key while dragging adds the fabric with physical properties only.  

The thick needle fabric effect is wider than ink material. I copy a piece using the loudspeaker and pattern and rename them “body” and “rip,” respectively, then apply the fabric to the pattern.  

The third step is pattern processing. First, prepare our pattern. There are two ways:  
1. Physical scan of the real paper or sweater, scanning front and back since the back pattern may differ.  
2. Generate pattern images from other software such as Apex (Shima Seiki), Adobe Substance, or Store. These can produce paper patterns and needle organization patterns.  

I do repeat needle organization patterns for the sweater. I open the folder in the texture and drag the twist pattern onto the large fabric, applying it alongside hairline and calligraphy images. You can adjust the shadow strength, with larger numbers increasing shadow intensity.  

The calligraphy image has color within the text, while the hairline image is generated by the system with an input strength value.  

For the calligraphy picture, a special processing is required in Photoshop because simple color adjustments don’t achieve the desired effect due to the black-and-white contrast and needle curve effects.  

In Photoshop, open the calligraphy picture, duplicate the layer to preserve the original, zoom in, and adjust brightness and contrast to increase distinction. Adjust color channels to enhance black and white division.  

Select black and white areas using the syllable lock tool or pen tool for contours. Adjust selected pixels to white by increasing brightness. Delete the white layer underneath and add a new black-filled layer with 80% opacity for smooth transitions.  

Merge layers and apply a blur effect to create a smooth black-to-white gradient to simulate the calligraphy effect, which is critical for the visual quality.  

This pattern corresponds to the feather plant pattern. Adjustments can be made for protruding areas.  

Next, edit sewing lines. Use the editing sewing line tool, select all sewing lines (Ctrl + A), and adjust their 3D strength to zero for a seamless effect. If sleeves are sewn, keep those lines active.  

Align patterns for side seams using print release mode and reset pattern arrangement. If seams are misaligned, select the panels and right-click to align their bottoms.  

Adjust fabric thickness, as our sweater fabric is thicker than the default 1.75 mm. Change it to 3 mm for a thicker effect and simulate to see the improved fold details and forceful appearance.  

Adjust collar line elasticity to control wrinkle tightness; 70-75% tail shrinkage provides a natural tightening effect.  

Shoulder, sleeve, and collar seams require fold angle adjustments using the editing sewing line tool to simulate inward folding and tuck effects. Folding angles of 180° create flat seams; 360° simulate tuck-ins. Adjust these angles and simulate to observe the effect.  

Turn on rendering to see the simulation with real-time lighting effects. Hair lines contribute significantly to the garment’s appearance.  

Adjust sound simulation to 2 mm and spiral simulation to 1 mm for better effect. Increase rendering size to view details clearly.  

For needlework effects, use wool thread material to support the sweater’s furry look. Change fabric type to hair and select Angora wool preset. Adjust hair length (default 30 too long, set to 0.02), thickness (hair thickness per strand), gravity effect (strength of hair bending), sharpness (transition from thick to thin), and density (hairs per inch, default 645).  

Lower density to 200 for a more suitable look, then render to review. Adjust hair thickness and transparency to improve visibility.  

Turn off skylight in rendering if background transparency is not clear. Adjust parameters like focus value (to minimum, e.g., 0.001), max render time, quality (set to very high), and rendering device (CPU or GPU depending on your hardware) to optimize hair rendering.  

Add subtle lighting to enhance light-colored hair visibility. Rendering hair materials takes longer than ordinary materials.  

Open the second costume model to demonstrate the use of light lines for twist details, especially at hair intersections. Create internal lines with three twists using the keyboard, then select line sections with the light line tool, adding single needles.  

Understand parameters: OBJ vs textual light lines (for self-defined light lines, use textual), key value (distance from the internal line; zero centers the line, positive moves right, negative moves left), length (length of single needle lines), evidence (distance between needles), and roughness (thickness of needles).  

Set units to centimeters for convenience.  

Apply self-defined name line with two-way continuous pictures replacing default text. Use pre-made two-way continuous twist effects corresponding to calligraphy, created as described earlier. Use colorless images so color can be added later without affecting the base.  

Adjust text size and proportions to match calligraphy size for consistency.  

Apply pink color to the costume and check for gaps caused by curves in the pattern; adjust negative gap values to close these gaps.  

Set line thickness to 1.2 and adjust overall effect parameters for flower collection effects.  

After adding calligraphy, adjust calligraphy intensity (e.g., big twist at 0.8 for 3D effect, 0.5 mm line width). If unfamiliar with calligraphy principles, refer to previous live broadcasts explaining calligraphy parameters in detail.  

The protruding effect comes from calligraphy processed from real scanned paper with high pixel resolution for better quality.  

Copy hair parameters to the new model and adjust color as needed.  

This sweater uses a thin needle fabric, so hair is short and small, not long and fuzzy. Render with improved quality for better detail.  

Finally, review how to create sweaters using the whole version. Some details cannot be done by line work alone and require scanning the entire pattern or importing patterns from other CAD software.  

After obtaining the pattern, close the sides and switch to print release mode to arrange fabric layout. Take a 1:1 snapshot for texturing.  

In Photoshop, perform detailed texture editing, including manual touch-ups for white areas and calligraphy.  

Apply textures back in CLO, adjusting resolution and ratio for proper alignment. Large images may cause software lag.  

For back texture, use stickers (whole pieces) applied to back panels in 2D window and add as stickers, adjusting position for full coverage to simulate back needle effect.  

Turn on rendering to check results, including twist and seam effects with white dots.  

Review the entire detail setting: fantasy image, hair settings for sweater hair length variation, self-defined name lines for flower details, seamless sewing line adjustments, thickness adjustments, and dyeing effects.  

This concludes today's content. If you have any questions about detail shapes or patterns, we can do a Q&A session. Playback will be available next week.  

Regarding information sharing, I can share the PPT of this process but not the materials, as you should be able to make your own sweater after this lecture.  

Regarding integration of needle, feather, and fabric functions, this idea has been acknowledged and responded to by our development team.  

Let me open a previously made sweater to avoid the screen feeling empty.  

If you want a close-up effect, the plate should be smaller and more flexible to better fit the model. You can adjust parameters for closer detail. New features can be developed practically; for example, a three-layer plate will be shaky, but that’s unrelated to today’s topic.  

Are there any questions about today’s topic?  

How to make feathers? Feathers are complex with many types. I might need to study this further as I haven’t done it before. I recall a bird feather I saw that can be made and adjusted by hair.  

It depends on the feather’s look and whether it’s based on fabric attributes or plate cutting. The plate and fabric attributes affect the outcome. If you stick plates, they tend to be smaller and less loose; fabric should be soft and stretchable.  

The CLO 7.0 automatic wearing function might not work if you haven’t found the correct method. There should be no problem; I can test it later and share the data next week along with the PPT.  

Please pay attention to our WeChat public number.  

You can actually do hook flower 3D hair today, but you need to have a hook flower 3D hair organization first. Then adjust the pattern organization accordingly.  

We use the board and apply tail shrinkage with added flexibility.  

Let me explain 3D detail manipulation using T-shirts as an example. In the 3D window, use the edit shape tool with the shrink shape line under the shape line tool. Select and click on the bottom, then drag to zoom in or adjust line length.  

The second twist is done with the line tool. You can see the twist clearly.  

If you like this video, please share it. I will be happy to create new videos.  

Thank you for watching. If there are no other questions, I will check online for answers to any remaining questions.  

If you want to know the chest circumference parameters of this clothing, you need to measure it yourself using the measurement point tool. Click points around the chest to measure circumference; double-click to complete the circle and see the value in the object window.  

Thank you.  

We will probably prepare another video covering topics you requested and prepare for the next video.  

I don’t see more questions. Why are people still joining the live stream? We are almost done!  

Okay, that’s all for today. Thank you, everyone. Bye-bye!  
Thanks for watching!

chunks.content: # CLO Master Express Lesson 25 Sweater Teaching Live Replay This document covers the detailed process of creating a sweater in CLO software, including garment construction methods, workflow steps, pattern preparation, 3D modeling techniques, fabric simulation, and advanced texture and needlework effects. It also explains key tools and parameters used in CLO for sweater design and simulation. --- ## Sweater Construction Methods and Overview This section explains the four primary garment construction methods used for sweaters in CLO, along with their 3D modeling applications and design expression. - **Cut and Sew:** Fabric pieces are cut and sewn together. This is one of the three main garment construction methods. - **Sew Each Piece Separately:** Fabric pieces are sewn individually without cutting, with patterns integrated into side materials. - **Bottom-Pattern Sewing:** Similar to the second method but involves sewing the pattern on the bottom with the fabric piece. - **One-Piece Shape:** The garment is created from a single piece without matching processes, sewn as a whole. All four methods utilize 3D modeling for design details, including flower collections, 3D organization, and gauze line characteristics, enabling rich design expression in CLO. --- ## Sweater Production Workflow This section outlines the three main workflow parts for sweater creation in CLO, covering digitalization, physicalization, fabric simulation, and physical processing. ### Workflow Parts: 1. **Digitalization:** - Use design software to create DXF paper patterns or pattern boards, essential as a base for 3D clothing creation in CLO. 2. **Physicalization:** - Scan real paper patterns if available, or manually draw pattern boards in CLO to create detailed pattern bases. 3. **Fabric Simulation:** - Simulate the physical properties of sweater fabric within CLO to replicate real fabric behavior. 4. **Physical Processing:** - Final adjustments and garment assembly in 3D, including sewing and structural modifications. --- ## Paper Sample Preparation Methods This section describes four methods to prepare paper samples (patterns) for sweater design in CLO: 1. **Using 2D CAD or 3D Software:** Generate paper samples externally and import into CLO. 2. **Adjusting DXF Samples:** Modify existing basic DXF paper samples for design changes. 3. **Direct Drawing in CLO:** Draw the paper sample manually according to measurement units. 4. **Collating Paper Samples:** Import and align existing paper samples within CLO for use. For this lesson, method two—modifying existing DXF samples—is used to create a basic sweater. --- ## 3D Model Adjustments and Tools This section explains the steps and tools used to modify the basic 3D sweater model in CLO, including resizing, shaping, and seam adjustments. - **Chest Volume Increase:** Collapse the basic chest line inward and align with the outer board line to prepare for cutting and sewing. - **Shrink Line Tool:** Allows direct manipulation of clothing lines in the 3D window. Press **Shift + Z** to display line length. Example: Shrinking by 25 units equals 2.5 cm (1 circle = 10 cm). - **Moving Shape Line Tool:** Adjusts lengths of pattern parts (e.g., shortening the bottom by 2 cm).

Adjust parameters: - Hair length (default 30 too long; set to 0.02) - Hair thickness per strand - Gravity effect (hair bending strength) - Sharpness (tapering from thick to thin) - Density (hairs per inch; default 645 reduced to 200 for better appearance) - Adjust hair thickness and transparency for visibility. - Turn off skylight if background transparency is unclear. - Set focus value to minimum (around 0.001). - Increase max render time and quality to “very high.” - Choose rendering device (CPU or GPU) based on hardware. - Add subtle lighting to enhance light-colored hair visibility. - Note: Hair rendering requires longer processing time than ordinary materials. --- ## Light Line and Twist Detail Application This section covers creating and adjusting light lines and twist details at hair intersections using CLO’s line tools. - Create internal lines with three twists using keyboard shortcuts. - Use the light line tool to select line sections and add single needles. - Understand key parameters: - OBJ vs Textual light lines (textual for self-defined light lines) - Key value: distance from internal line (0 = center, positive = right, negative = left) - Length: length of single needle lines - Evidence: spacing between needles - Roughness: needle thickness - Set units to centimeters for convenience. - Apply self-defined name lines with two-way continuous twist images replacing default text. - Use colorless images for flexibility in color adjustments. - Adjust text size and proportion to match calligraphy size. - Apply color (e.g., pink) to the costume. - Adjust negative gap values to close curve-induced gaps. - Set line thickness (e.g., 1.2) and overall parameters for flower collection effects. - Adjust calligraphy intensity and line width for 3D effects (e.g., 0.8 intensity, 0.5 mm line width). -
